title: Chapter 146 – The Hollow Gold
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The formula runs to eleven lines, and Head Yan Rongzhi reads it aloud three times before he will let anyone else touch the paper.

They are in the ridge-house, in the long cold hall where the Chain once slept, now swept clean and turned into a school. Thirty children sit in rows on the old jade slabs, copying characters, under the eye of a stern young pupil. At the far end, by the window, the Head sits in his wooden chair with a blanket across his knees, white hair brushed back, and spectacles that Lu Fei had made for him from the lenses of a broken telescope. He has been awake for eleven years. He looks, Jian sometimes thinks, ten years younger for it.

"Again," says Jian.

"You have heard it twice."

"Once more."

"Very well." The Head lifts the sheet. It is the oiled paper from the box of broken lamps, the one with the scratched-out name in the margin, and the writing on it is small and upright and cramped. "A seed is not a stone. It is a promise a stone makes. To plant it, find the hollow place in the body's own gold, the place that was already waiting. Put the seed in the hollow. Feed it every night for fourteen years from the same well that feeds the body. At the end, the hollow will be a core, and the body will be a man who has learned to carry himself."

"Fourteen years."

"Fourteen." The black eyes come up over the spectacles. "The first line is the one that matters. The place that was already waiting. Do you know what it means?"

"The Seal."

"The Seal." Yan Rongzhi lays the page down. "I have a theory, Keeper. Not a proof. When I lay on that slab for seventy years, the Fire burned in me, and I had a great deal of time to look at it. I came to think that the whole of the Sect's gold, the Core that every disciple seeks, is only a poor imitation of something your interface made, a long time ago. A cheap copy of a hollow that was cut for you, by someone who knew you would need it."

"Ethan Cole."

"If that is his name." The old man's mouth twists. "I do not claim to understand it. But I think it is no accident that the formula speaks of a hollow already waiting. The Seal is the only hollow in you that is not yours."

Jian looks at the paper. He has been reading it for a week. The words do not change. Feed it every night. That is the cost. The Reservoir, the cell, the labor of every evening of his life for fourteen years, poured down a single drain. There will be nothing left for anyone else.

"I know what you are going to say," says the Head.

"What?"

"That you cannot do it. That your father is ninety-nine years old and has been cold for twelve of them. That your sister is fifty-seven and going gray. That your mother has a long way left to walk, and the Reservoir is the only road any of them have." He tilts his head. "Am I close?"

"You are exact."

"Then I will tell you what the other Keeper would have said." He taps the page. "Plant the seed."

* * *

Lin Zhao brings her son to the ridge-house on the fourth day, wrapped in a blue blanket, to be shown to the Head.

It is not an official visit. She has no particular reason to come; the baby is three weeks old and sleeps through everything. But she is thirty-one, with her mother's tilted head and her grandfather's long jaw, and she has the look of a young woman who has decided to do something sentimental and does not intend to be argued out of it. She stops in the doorway of the long hall. She looks at Jian, at the white hair, and her eyes go wide and soft.

"Uncle. May I?"

"Of course."

She crosses the hall and puts the bundle into his arms before he can reply. He has not held an infant in thirty years. It is astonishingly heavy for something so small, warm and boneless and smelling of milk, and when it opens its eyes they are dark, wide and perfectly unimpressed.

"What is his name?"

"We have not said." Zhao glances at her husband, standing in the door in his Court gray, looking like a man who wishes to be elsewhere. "We thought, Uncle, if you would not mind... we thought of Kuang."

He does not answer for a moment. The baby yawns, with the whole of its small body, a huge pink pinched yawn, and goes slack.

"He would not mind," he says at last. "He would not know what to say. He would go red and pretend to cough." His throat tightens, and it is a wonderful sensation, the tightening. "Lin Kuang."

"Lin Kuang," says Zhao. She smiles, with her whole face, and he sees Yue in her, and Qinghe, and, behind them both, a hundred stubborn years of apple trees and onions. "It is a very good name for someone who is going to stand in the middle of things."

Across the room, the Head has put down his spectacles. He is looking at the child with great attention, and then at Jian, and then at the child again.

"Pass him here," he says.

"Master Yan?"

"I am an old man, and the only thing I have ever wanted to hold since I woke is a baby that does not know what year it is." He holds out his thin arms. "I promise not to drop him."

* * *

He does not decide that day. He does not decide for a month.

It is the hardest decision of his life, and he knows it. There is no villain in it. There is no knife at anyone's throat. There is only a column of figures, which he can recite in his sleep, and which comes out the same every night.

The Core Seed needs a hundred CE over the first year, and forty points of Seal. The Reservoir, at sixty, will not cover it. He will have to labor: two CE a night, as always, and the Spring Vein, and everything he can scrape from the ordinary world. For fourteen years the whole of his surplus goes down the Seed's throat. Wenyuan's step to Late stands at one hundred and twenty. Yue's step needs nothing but the jar, but the jar has its own price. Qinghe has said, flatly, that she will not ask. Feng will not ask either, and Feng is the one who has not slept in a decade.

He does not say that aloud. But he has begun to hear what Yue hears, the low hum beneath the world, and under it, in his brother's chest, a thin fast flutter, the sound of a man worn down to the wire.

On the thirty-first night, he goes to the orchard and sits under the Mother Tree's daughter with his back to the trunk. It is early spring. The buds have not opened. The snow lies in patches on the black grass, and the air smells of wet earth and wood-smoke, and he has the sense, strong and absurd, that he is waiting for someone.

Wenyuan finds him there.

The old man comes slowly, on his apple-wood staff, wrapped to the chin in a quilted gown, with a lantern. He is ninety-nine. His cold hands are bare, and they shine like marble in the light. He lowers himself onto the grass with a groan and sits beside his son with his back against the same trunk, and for a long time neither of them says anything at all.

"I know what you are afraid of," says Wenyuan at last.

"I am not afraid."

"Of course you are. You get a look." He sniffs. "You had it when you were six. You had broken the good bowl and you hid the pieces under the bed, and sat there with your arms around your knees. It is the very same look."

Jian laughs, despite himself.

"Listen to me, boy." Wenyuan turns his long face. His eyes are damp and bright. "I have lived ninety-nine years. I was a poor man's son and a fool, and I lost everything, and I came back to this hill with a baby and a wife and a cart. I have had more than I ever deserved. Do you think I want more?"

"I—"

"I want you to plant your seed." He says it quietly, firmly, with the unarguable weight of a man making his last request. "That is all. I do not want a hundred and twenty. I do not want the Reservoir. If I am to walk another step, I will walk it by my own feet, in my own time. And if I am not..." He shrugs. "Then I was there for a good deal. I saw a great many apples."

"Father—"

"I will not hear it." The old hand closes on Jian's wrist with surprising strength. "Little stone. Everyone in this family has been giving you a piece of themselves since the day you came. Your mother her taste. Your brother his sleep. Your sister her hearing. And you have been giving it away again, one piece at a time, to anyone who asked." His voice breaks. "Let somebody give you one thing back. Let us give you the time."

Jian cannot speak. He puts his arm around the old man's shoulders, and Wenyuan leans against him, small and cold and weightless in the quilted gown, and in the dark the buds on the Mother Tree's daughter swell, one by one, like a held breath.

* * *

Qinghe takes longer to persuade, and does it in a different way.

She comes to the Dock. She has not been there in thirty years, and she walks down the seven hundred and one steps with her chin up, in her blue smock, with a lantern, and stands in the vast dim round room at the foot of the stair, looking at the Gate wall. She does not say anything for some time. Then she says, in a perfectly ordinary voice, "It is smaller than I thought."

"It is a wall."

"It is a door." She walks up to it and lays a small hand against the stone. "I have heard about it all my life. I have wondered what all the fuss was." She turns. Her sharp eyes find him in the gloom. "Where will you put it?"

"The Seed?"

"Your gold."

"Here." He indicates the floor in front of the wall: a plain flat stone, worn smooth by three hundred years of Keepers. "I will have to sit within reach of the Gate. The Seal needs to be near the source."

"For how long?"

"Fourteen years. A night at a time."

She nods slowly. She walks back to him, and her face in the lantern light is calm and sad and a little amused.

"You are going to be here every night."

"Yes."

"For fourteen years."

"Yes."

"Then I shall bring you supper." She sets the lantern on the floor. "I'll not have a man planting gold on an empty stomach. And I shall want a chair. A good one. With a back."

"Mother, it is a damp dark cellar—"

"Jian." She has the tone she used on him when he was eight. "I am ninety-one years old. I have no sense of taste, and I have a very small number of things left in my life that I can do for you. Bringing you supper is one of them. Do not take it away."

He looks at her. After a moment, he bows his head.

"Thank you."

"Good." She pats his cheek. "Now go and plant your seed."

* * *

Yue comes to him on the thirty-fourth night, in the Dock, while he is testing the flat stone with his boot.

Qinghe has sent down a trial supper in a covered basket: rice, pickled radish, a boiled egg, and a piece of dried fish that smells so strongly of salt that he can taste it through the cloth. He sets it on the flat stone. He is about to sit when his sister's lantern bobs down the last of the stairs, and she steps off the bottom with her head cocked and her sleeves rolled to the elbow.

"Hum's changed," she says.

"Has it?"

"It was a low D. A kind of... sleeping D. Now there is a second note over it, very faint." She hums it, a thin, true, strange little sound. "I do not know what it is. But it sounds like a seed."

"It is."

"I thought so." She leans against the wall, arms folded. Her hair is gray now, drawn into a plain braid, and the lines at the corners of her eyes are deep. She is fifty-seven. She has the quiet watchful manner of a woman who has listened to things all her life. "Brother. I have to ask you something, and I would like a real answer."

"Ask."

"Jar one. The one you took for me from the Dock Five pantry." She does not look at him. "The ear."

His hand stops on the basket.

"Feng told me," she says. "He heard you speak of it to Father. He wasn't spying. He cannot help it, and neither can I." Her mouth twists. "You were going to give it to me, weren't you? After the Seed. When it was safe."

"Yes."

"Then I would like you to know I am not going to wait."

"Yue—"

"I am fifty-seven, Jian. Mother is ninety-one. Father is ninety-nine. They are not going to be here forever, whatever the rule, and I have a hum in my head that has been growing for thirty years, and I do not know what it is for." She turns, finally. Her eyes are very bright. "I think the jar was meant for me. I think the label said so. For the one who hears. I should like to know what I am for."

He thinks of the label. He thinks of the corridor in the light, and the small pale figure in the white shirt. He thinks of his own two signatures, and the knowledge that there are questions in the world he can answer only by asking the person who is not there.

"It has a price," he says. "I do not know what it is. The Docks never say."

"No."

"Will you pay it?"

"I'll pay it," says Yue. "I paid for everything else."

He swallows. Then he nods. "After the Seed takes root. Give me a month, and I will give you the jar. I want you to have the best chance." He hesitates. "And I want it to be a real choice. Not one I make for you."

"Nobody has made a choice for me in thirty years." She smiles crookedly. "That is what a bell is, little brother. It rings when somebody else decides to pull."

* * *

Lu Fei brings the readings on the thirty-sixth night, with her roll under one arm and a flask of hot barley tea in the other.

She is forty-eight now, and Second Chair of the Sect under Head Han, and the Hall of Weights has been hers for six years. She has not softened. She still looks at the world as at a document that someone has copied badly. She spreads the sheets on the table in the ridge-house, weighs the corners with the flask and the lamp and a chunk of ink, and says, "You will not like the second page."

"I rarely do."

"The Dock's pulse is strong. It has been strong since the waking. That is the first page." She taps. "The Gate wall is not resting. Since the Archivist stopped speaking, it has made a sound I have never recorded before, and the line on this chart is what it makes."

Jian looks. The line is not ragged, and not flat. It is a long, slow, perfectly regular wave, like the breathing of a sleeper.

"It is waiting," says Lu Fei.

"For what?"

"I would say for you." She meets his eyes. "I have been in this Sect since I was nine, Keeper. I have read every reading that Cheng Yun wrote and every one that came after. In all that time I have never seen a wall do what that wall is doing now. It is tuning. Like a man tuning an instrument, before a performance."

"Of what?"

"I cannot say. But if you put a seed in your Seal and sit before it every night for fourteen years, I think the wall will tune itself to you." She rolls up the sheets, very precisely. "I do not know if that is good. I know that it is true."

He considers this. It is the same thing the Head said, in different words. The Gate will answer. He had thought it a figure of speech.

"Thank you, Second Chair."

"Do not mention it." She tucks the roll under her arm, and pauses at the door, with her back to him, small and stiff and very straight. "Keeper. The boy, Tian Mo. The one who stands. He asked me last week whether he could stand watch at the Dock, on the nights you are there."

"Stand watch?"

"He says that it is the kind of thing Master Kuang would have done." She does not turn. "I said I would ask."

Jian is quiet for a while.

"Tell him yes," he says. "Tell him he may stand as long as he likes. And that if the Gate should ever come for me in the night, I should like him to be the wall."

On the thirty-eighth night he packs his room.

It takes less time than it should. A cot, a quilt, a lamp. A chipped teapot that was Bai's. A small folded cloth, blue, that was Sang Ruo's. Ye's black stick, which Pei Wanli pressed into his hands at the funeral and which he has never found a place to put. He wraps them in a bundle and carries them down the seven hundred and one steps one load at a time, with Pebble riding on his shoulder, and sets them out along the south wall of the Dock in a little crooked row.

It looks like the camp of a man who intends to stay a long time.

"This is foolish," says Pebble.

"Yes."

"You have a house. A bed. A mother who cooks."

"I do."

"You could sit here for three hours a night and walk home to sleep."

"I could." Jian sets down the teapot. "But the Seed likes to be fed at the same hour, and I will be too tired to climb that stair. And I would rather be here when the Gate answers." He straightens, with a hand at the small of his back, and looks at the long hard crack that runs down the creature's gray spine. "How is the back?"

"The same."

"Does it hurt?"

"It hums." The black eyes blink slowly. "Like the girl. A different note. I think it is trying to become a door."

Jian says nothing. He sits on the cot and looks at the wall for a long time.

* * *

Jar 2 sits on a table in the middle of his room, and he has not opened it in eleven years.

He takes it out of the cabinet on the fortieth night, and carries it down the seven hundred and one steps in both hands, like a man carrying a sleeping child. It is a plain heavy jar of grayish ceramic, sealed with wax, no bigger than a rice bowl, and on the lid is a symbol he took, long ago, for a cooking mark. Two overlapping circles, one empty, one filled.

Hollow Gold, the label says, in Ethan Cole's scrawl. Core Seed catalyst. For when you're ready. It won't be soon. I'm sorry.

He sets it on the flat stone before the Gate wall. He sits down cross-legged. He lays his hands on his knees. Behind him, on the stair, a lantern bobs, and a small figure in a blue smock comes down the last step with a basket on her arm and a stool, which she plants against the wall with great firmness. Beyond her, Wenyuan in his quilt. Beyond him, Yue, with her head cocked. Beyond her, Feng, thin and quiet, with his hand pressed to his ribs.

They do not speak. They have come to witness. That is all.

Jian breaks the wax.

The smell that rises is not what he expected. It is not metallic. It is not even strange. It smells like a field after rain: warm, green, faintly sweet. He tips the jar, and a thread of liquid light comes out, slow and heavy as honey, the color of morning in the Orchard. It pools in the cup of his palm. It is warm. It is, absurdly, the temperature of a hand.

```
ARK-3 :: CORE SEED METHOD
CATALYST: Hollow Gold (jar 2) ........ PRESENT
LEVEL: Purple Mansion Peak ........... OK
SEAL: 81% .......................... OK
SEAT: Dock Primary (Gate within reach) OK
PLANTING DRAW: 42 Seal / 18 CE (initial)
NIGHTLY FEED: 2 CE (14 years = 5,110 nights)
RESERVOIR LINK: locked to Seed for duration
COLE DOOR: will not close after Core. NOTE: NOT REVERSIBLE.
WARNING: Seed visible to Gate. Gate will answer.
CONFIRM [Y/N]
```

He reads the last warning twice.

Gate will answer.

In the vast dim room, at the other side of the wall, something stirs. It is not a sound. It is the opposite of a sound, the pressure change that comes before a storm, a slow settling of the air as of a great thing turning its attention. His family feels it too. Qinghe's hand goes to her throat. Yue closes her eyes.

Plant the seed, says the Head, in his head. Plant it.

Let us give you the time, says his father.

He sets the light on his tongue.

* * *

It does not hurt. That is the first surprise.

He had expected it to burn. Everything burns, in the end, in cultivation, the breaking and the building, but the Hollow Gold goes down his throat like warm milk, and settles in his stomach, and begins, very slowly, to spread. It runs along the three tracks of Qi and Body and Soul. It finds the Seal at the center of him, that cold bright locked place that has been his since the first night in Reed Courtyard, and it settles into it the way a bird settles into a nest.

There is a hollow there. He has always known it. A little round place, smaller than a thumb, that has never been quite filled. For nine years he had thought it was his grief. It is not. It is a place that was cut for this.

Mine, the Seal seems to say. Mine, mine.

The light goes in. He feels it go. He feels the Seal take it, and close around it, and the hollow fill with a small, steady, golden hum, like the first note of a very long song.

```
SEED PLANTED.
SEAL: 81% -> 41%
RESERVOIR: 60 -> 42 (Seed draw)
CELL: 6 -> 2
NIGHT 1 OF 5,110 :: FEED 2 CE
COLE DOOR: PAGE 2 LOCKED (Seal < 60%). Reopens at Seal 60%.
```

He sags forward onto his hands. Qinghe is beside him instantly, with a cloth, and he lets her wipe his face, and tastes salt, and realizes that he is weeping again, easily, helplessly, like a boy.

"It is in," he says.

"I know." She holds his head against her shoulder. "I felt it too. A kind of... click. Like a lid."

"It will take fourteen years."

"Then we shall have fourteen years." She rocks him slightly. "Hush. Hush. You are very tired."

Behind them, in the vast dim room, the Gate wall is knocking.

It is a slow, soft, deliberate sound. One. A pause. Two. Then three, quite distinct, like the knuckles of a polite visitor on a very old door. Yue lifts her head. Feng, at the back, has gone white.

"Brother," he says hoarsely. "That's not the solstice."

"No," says Jian.

"It's the Archivist."

"Yes." He straightens, slowly, and looks at the stone. His face, in the lantern light, is thin and white-haired and weary, and quite calm. "He told me once that he knew what the door was. I think he has just seen it open."

The knocking stops.

From the Gate wall, very faintly, from somewhere on the other side of six hundred years of stone, comes a voice. Pleasant. Tired. Almost kind.

Plant it, Keeper, says the Archivist. Plant it well. I shall be here when it flowers.
